extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Renaissance satire and classic literature (readers of Rabelais)
extracted.subtask_description: An English translation excerpt from Rabelais' Gargantua & Pantagruel containing narrative episodes, moral and legal observations, and satirical commentary rather than an explicit how-to or formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning criteria for Bridlegoose
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel pleads that Bridlegoose should be pardoned because of his old age, his simplicity, and the many just sentences he has already given: 'In the first place, his old age; secondly, his simplicity... that this one, sole, and single fault of his ought to be quite forgotten, abolished, and swallowed up by that immense and vast ocean of just dooms and sentences which heretofore he hath given and pronounced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel proposes conditional pardon: 'First, that he satisfy, or put a sufficient surety for the satisfaction of the party wronged... And, secondly, that for his subsidiary aid... you would be pleased to appoint and assign unto him some pretty little virtuous counsellor, younger, learneder, and wiser than he... or otherwise, if you intend totally to depose him... I shall cordially entreat you to make a present and free gift of him to me.' (Includes rationale: prior long record of uprightness, divine benignity confirming past sentences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of aleatory (dice) decision in law
rubrics_metrics.description: The text reports Bridlegoose's admission that he determined suits 'by the mere chance and fortune of the dice' and treats this as a subject for judgment: 'who... hath plainly confessed his final judging and determinating of suits of law by the mere chance and fortune of the dice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel and others defend the practice in certain circumstances: 'Who had decided that plea by the chance and fortune of the dice, could not have erred... If against the woman, she deserved punishment... If for her, the just resentment... did fully excuse her.' Pantagruel conjectures that in cases of antinomies and perplexity a judge may 'throw and turn the dice, to the end that by the providence aforesaid the best chance might fall to him whose action was uprightest.' Talmudic and providential justification (little harm, divine manifestation of will) are invoked as supporting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When confronted with insoluble legal perplexities, consult or defer
rubrics_metrics.description: Faced with an inextricable case (the Smyrna woman), the proconsul 'sent to the Areopagites then sitting at Athens to learn and obtain their advice and judgment' and the Areopagites' reply was effectively to defer: summon her to appear 'a precise hundred years thereafter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative suggests practical responses to knotty disputes: seek higher/collective counsel (Areopagus), defer decision if the matter is truly inextricable, or resort to procedures (including, in the story's world, aleatory methods) when reason cannot safely decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of prophetic/vatic inspiration (head-shaking etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triboulet's shaking and wagging of the head is interpreted as evidence of prophetic inspiration: 'such a brangling agitation and moving should by us all be judged to proceed from, and be quickened and suscitated by the coming and inspiration of the prophetizing and fatidical spirit... a little frenzy and a head-shaking' is concomitant with vaticination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives classical and anecdotal exemplars (Pythian divineress, Heliogabalus, Plautus, Catullus, Bacchic women, Galli), and records Julian's remark that absence of head-wagging might indicate soundness; physicians and ancient authorities are cited to explain trembling as either bodily weakness or sign of possession/inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage should not be contracted by children without parental consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Gargantua asserts a normative rule: 'I never yet heard that by any law... it was allowed and approved of that children may be suffered and tolerated to marry at their own goodwill and pleasure, without the knowledge, advice, or consent asked and had thereto of their fathers, mothers, and nearest kindred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He adds that 'All legislators, everywhere upon the face of the whole earth, have taken away and removed this licentious liberty from children, and totally reserved it to the discretion of the parents.' The passage functions as an explicit social/legal standard (parental control over children's marriages) and criticizes sacerdotal interference in secular family law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial integrity: avoid selling laws and corrupt manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The text condemns those who corrupt legal process and 'sell laws': 'their principal direction in all law matters comes to their hands from one Tribonian, a wicked, miscreant... it was his ordinary custom to sell laws, edicts, declarations, constitutions, and ordinances, as at an outroop or putsale, to him who offered most for them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative critique: such practices 'conceal, suppress, disannull, and abolish' parts of law to serve private ends; transparency and fidelity to the whole law are implied as standards for just administration. Rabelais frames corruption as a cause of injustice and as worse than relying on aleatory methods.
